title: WHAT IS THE REAL MEANING OF CARRYING YOUR CROSS?
paragraphs: WHAT IS THE REAL MEANING OF CARRYING YOUR CROSS?
The Verse Almost Everyone Gets Wrong
By Gospel Warrior
Most people think carrying your cross means dealing with difficult people.
A difficult marriage.
A difficult boss.
A chronic illness.
Financial pressure.
Personal struggles.
We hear people say things like, “Well, that's just my cross to bear.”
But when Jesus first spoke those words, nobody listening thought about inconvenience.
Nobody thought about hardship.
Nobody thought about life's frustrations.
They thought about death.
Because in the first century, a man carrying a cross was not someone managing problems.
He was someone walking toward execution.
That changes everything.
The words of Jesus have become so familiar that many believers no longer feel the weight of them.
But if we return to the original language, the historical setting, and the shocking reality behind His command, we discover something that may completely transform how we understand discipleship.
And perhaps expose why so many people want Jesus as Savior while resisting Him as Lord.
The Day Jesus Said Something Nobody Wanted to Hear
Jesus declared:

“If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me.”
(Luke 9:23)
The Greek text reads:
"εἴ τις θέλει ὀπίσω μου ἔρχεσθαι, ἀπαρνησάσθω ἑαυτόν καὶ ἀράτω τὸν σταυρὸν αὐτοῦ καθ’ ἡμέραν καὶ ἀκολουθείτω μοι"
Transliteration:
Ei tis thelei opisō mou erchesthai, aparnēsasthō heauton kai aratō ton stauron autou kath’ hēmeran kai akoloutheitō moi.
The phrase "ἀπαρνησάσθω ἑαυτόν" (aparnēsasthō heauton) means more than simply practicing self-discipline.
It literally means to deny ownership of oneself.
To renounce personal claims.
To surrender the throne of your own life.
Then comes the command:
"ἀράτω τὸν σταυρὸν αὐτοῦ"
"Take up his cross."
The word used for cross is "σταυρός" (stauros).
To modern readers, the cross often represents jewelry, church decorations, artwork, or inspirational symbolism.
To first-century listeners, it represented torture, shame, humiliation, rejection, and death.
There was no positive association.
None.
A cross was Rome's public declaration that a person's will had been completely conquered.
When Jesus told His followers to carry theirs, He was calling them into radical surrender.
Not comfort.
Not convenience.
Not self-improvement.
Surrender.
The Forgotten Horror Behind the Cross
Today we see crosses hanging in churches.
In Jesus' day, crosses stood beside roads.
Covered in blood.
Covered in flies.
Covered in dying men.
The Roman Empire intentionally made crucifixion public.
It was designed to terrify.
It was a warning.
A message.
Submit or suffer.
When condemned prisoners carried the horizontal beam through the streets, everyone knew what it meant.
The verdict had already been decided.
The man carrying the cross was not negotiating his future.
His future had already been surrendered.
That image is exactly what Jesus used.
Not by accident.
Not poetically.
Intentionally.
He chose the most shocking image available.
Because true discipleship is not adding Jesus to your existing plans.
It is surrendering your plans entirely.
The Problem Modern Christianity Rarely Talks About
Many people want a Jesus who helps them achieve their dreams.
But biblical discipleship begins when our dreams are placed on the altar.
Jesus never invited people merely to improve their lives.
He invited them to die.
Not physically in every case.
But spiritually.
The Apostle Paul later captured this truth when he wrote:

“I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me.”
(Galatians 2:20)
The Greek says:
"Χριστῷ συνεσταύρωμαι"
Transliteration:
Christō synestaurōmai.
Literally:
"I have been crucified together with Christ."
Paul did not describe Christianity as behavior modification.
He described it as participation in a death.
The death of self-rule.
The death of self-worship.
The death of personal sovereignty.
And from that death emerges something entirely new.
The Life Most People Never Experience
This is where many believers become trapped.
They try to follow Jesus while preserving complete control.
They want salvation without surrender.
Forgiveness without obedience.
Grace without transformation.
But carrying your cross means something far deeper.
It means surrendering your right to be your own god.
Every day.
Every decision.
Every relationship.
Every ambition.
Every hidden desire.
Every secret idol.
Every fear.
Every wound.
Every dream.
Placed before Christ.
Not because He wants less for you.
But because He wants infinitely more than your limited vision can imagine.
The Aramaic Heart Behind the Teaching
Jesus primarily taught in Aramaic.
Although the New Testament preserves His teachings in Greek, scholars generally recognize that many sayings originated in Aramaic speech patterns.
The concept behind carrying one's cross is closely connected to complete submission to God's authority.
A central Aramaic expression Jesus used repeatedly was:
"אבא"
Abba.
Father.
Not merely as a title.
But as an expression of trust and surrender.
The One carrying the cross is not walking toward meaningless suffering.
He is walking with trust toward the Father.
The same trust Jesus demonstrated in Gethsemane when He prayed:

“Not my will, but yours, be done.”
(Luke 22:42)
Those words may be the clearest picture of carrying a cross ever recorded.
Before Jesus carried a physical cross, He carried a surrendered heart.
That is where every cross-bearing life begins.
The Cross You Carry May Not Look Like What You Expected
Sometimes carrying your cross means forgiving someone who never apologized.
Sometimes it means remaining faithful when compromise seems easier.
Sometimes it means standing for biblical truth when culture turns hostile.
Sometimes it means surrendering a relationship God has forbidden.
Sometimes it means obeying when obedience costs you popularity.
Sometimes it means remaining faithful when nobody notices.
Sometimes it means saying yes to God when your flesh desperately wants to say no.
The cross is not merely suffering.
Many people suffer.
The cross is surrendered suffering.
There is a difference.
The Question That Changes Everything
When Jesus carried His cross, He knew where the road led.
Calvary.
Yet He kept walking.
Not because nails held Him.
Love held Him.
And every follower of Christ eventually arrives at the same question:
What am I still refusing to surrender?
Because the cross is not merely something we carry.
It is something that exposes us.
It reveals whether Jesus is truly Lord or merely an addition to our lives.
The cross reveals what we love most.
The cross reveals what we trust most.
The cross reveals who truly sits on the throne.
Perhaps that is why Jesus never softened the invitation.
He loved people too much to offer them a counterfeit gospel.
The Beautiful Ending Nobody Saw Coming
The story does not end with a cross.
It never did.
The cross always leads somewhere.
The tomb.
And then beyond the tomb.
Resurrection.
This is the promise hidden inside Jesus' command.
Every surrendered thing placed in His hands becomes a place where resurrection power can work.
The death of pride becomes humility.
The death of addiction becomes freedom.
The death of bitterness becomes healing.
The death of self-rule becomes peace.
The death of old identity becomes new creation.
The cross feels like losing.
Until resurrection arrives.
Then you realize it was the pathway to life all along.
Maybe that is why Jesus said:

“For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it.”
(Luke 9:24)
The Greek word for life here is:
"ψυχή" (psychē)
Often translated soul, life, self, or inner being.
The paradox is breathtaking.
The person desperately protecting self ultimately loses self.
The person surrendering self to Christ ultimately discovers who they were created to be.
That is the real meaning of carrying your cross.
Not enduring inconvenience.
Not surviving hardship.
Not tolerating difficult circumstances.
It is the daily surrender of self to the Lordship of Jesus Christ.
It is dying before you die.
So you can finally live.
And maybe while reading this, you realized there is something you are still holding back.
Something Christ has been asking you to surrender.
A relationship.
A habit.
A fear.
A secret.
A wound.
A dream.
A piece of your heart you have not fully placed in His hands.
Be honest.
What is your cross right now?
Your testimony may be the encouragement someone else desperately needs.
One day you will discover that the hardest thing you ever surrendered was also the doorway God used to give you life.
